# Architecture claim verification checklist

> Generated by `npm run verify:report` from `content/`. Do not edit by hand; record results with the commands below and regenerate.

**Progress:** 0 / 683 claims fully verified · 0 verified, 849 unverified, 0 incorrect, 0 unsupported (849 claim–source checks).

## How to verify

1. Open the source URL. Each section below is one source page with every claim that cites it.
2. For each claim, find the sentence on the page that supports it. Numbers must match (rounding like "about" is fine; a different figure is not).
3. Record the result (or fill in the CSV and run `npm run verify:import-csv -- docs/verification/architecture.csv --by "Your Name"`):
   - **verified**: the page states it. Paste the supporting sentence as the quote.
   - **unsupported**: the page does not say it. Find a better source or change the claim.
   - **incorrect**: the page (or better evidence) contradicts it. The card/question must be revised in a new revision.
4. A level can only be published when every claim it states or teaches is verified against every source it cites. `npm run validate:content` enforces this.

"Pre-check" notes were written while drafting. They point at what to look at closely. They are not verification.

"Fact-check" results come from an automated check against independent sources found by web search (not the cited page, which couldn't be opened). A **corrected** or **disputed** claim was reworded to match those sources; the old wording is shown. They are not verification either: the cited page still has to be checked.

- **Source:** `source.ada_2010_standards`
- **URL:** https://www.ada.gov/law-and-regs/design-standards/2010-stds/
- **License:** US_gov_public_domain · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.architecture.future_ada_ramp_slope`: unverified

> **Claim:** The 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design require ramp runs to have a running slope no steeper than 1:12, one unit of rise for every 12 of run.

- **Concept:** The 1:12 ramp (`concept.architecture.future_ramp_slope`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L98 “Design for Everyone” · `card.architecture.098.c3` (text): The one-in-twelve rule / Some of it is plain arithmetic. The 2010 ADA Standards, the US accessibility rules, say a ramp run can be no steeper than 1:12: every inch of rise needs at least 12 inches of ramp. So a 6-inch step becomes a 6-foot ramp. Try it in your head with the front steps of your home.
- **Tested by:**
  - L98 `question.architecture.098.q1`: Under the 2010 ADA Standards, what is the steepest slope allowed for a ramp run? → **1:12**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The US Access Board's guide to ramps and curb ramps gives the same 1:12 maximum running slope. Sources: https://www.access-board.gov/ada/guides/chapter-4-ramps-and-curb-ramps/, https://www.ada.gov/resources/2010-stds-guidance/

```sh
npm run verify:record -- fact.architecture.future_ada_ramp_slope source.ada_2010_standards --status verified --by "Your Name" --quote "…"
```

### ☐ `fact.architecture.sky_sullivan_essay`: unverified

> **Claim:** In his 1896 essay 'The Tall Office Building Artistically Considered', Louis Sullivan wrote that 'form ever follows function': a grand, open street floor, identical office tiers made to look alike 'because they are all alike', and an attic that shows the offices have ended.

- **Concept:** Sullivan: form follows function (`concept.architecture.sky_sullivan_form`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L61 “The First Skyscrapers” · `card.architecture.061.c4` (text): Form ever follows function / A frame could stand tall. But what should a tall building look like? In an 1896 essay, Louis Sullivan answered: "form ever follows function." Give the street floor a grand entrance and big openings for shops. Above it, stack the offices, and since every office is alike, make every window alike, "because they are all alike." Then top it with an attic that shows the offices have ended. The outside tells you what's inside.
- **Tested by:**
  - L61 `question.architecture.061.q1`: In his 1896 essay on the tall office building, what did Louis Sullivan say to do with the windows of the office floors? → **Make them all alike, because the offices are all alike**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Wikipedia's 'Form follows function' article dates the phrase to Sullivan's 1896 Lippincott's essay; ArchDaily republishes the essay with the same three-part argument. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Form_follows_function, https://www.archdaily.com/773283/the-long-ish-read-louis-sullivan-discusses-the-tall-office-artistically-considered

> **Claim:** Sullivan stressed a tall building's vertical elements and minimized its horizontals, to make it a 'proud and soaring' unity.

## On the Structure of the Roman Pantheon (The Art Bulletin 68:1, 1986) (Robert Mark and Paul Hutchinson, The Art Bulletin (Taylor & Francis))

- **Source:** `source.artbulletin_pantheon_structure`
- **URL:** https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/00043079.1986.10788309
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.architecture.wonders_pantheon_crack_pattern`: unverified

> **Claim:** The Pantheon's dome has cracks running top to rim through its lower half; they stop short of the oculus, the round opening at the top. Robert Mark and Paul Hutchinson analyzed this in 1986.

- **Concept:** The Pantheon's cracked dome (`concept.architecture.wonders_pantheon_cracks`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L19 “The Pantheon” · `card.architecture.019.c1` (text): The Pantheon's dome is cracked. It has stood for almost 1,900 years anyway. / Level 7 named it the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome, about 43 m across. Level 5 predicted where masonry domes crack. So why is this one still up?
  - L19 “The Pantheon” · `card.architecture.019.c3` (text): Cracks, right where Level 5 said / Remember Level 5: in a masonry dome, the hoop forces stretch toward the base, and domes tend to crack into slices. The Pantheon did exactly that. Its cracks run top to rim through the lower half of the dome, and they stop short of the oculus, the round opening at the top. ### ☐ `fact.architecture.future_clt_both_ways`: unverified

> **Claim:** Cross-laminating gives CLT dimensional stability and strength and stiffness in both directions, so it can make wide, long floor slabs and walls.

- **Concept:** Cross-laminated timber (`concept.architecture.future_clt`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L93 “Tall Timber” · `card.architecture.093.c2` (text): Boards, crossed and glued / The key product is cross-laminated timber, or CLT: layers of lumber boards stacked crosswise, typically at right angles, and glued together, at least three layers thick. It was introduced in the early 1990s in Austria and Germany. Crossing the layers is the whole point. A crossed panel is stable, strong and stiff in both directions, so it can make wide floor slabs and whole walls. Here's an analogy: a woven mat holds together far better than a pile of loose straws.
- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Think Wood says gluing layers at right angles gives CLT structural rigidity in both directions; naturally:wood says the cross lamination provides stability, strength and rigidity. Sources: https://www.thinkwood.com/mass-timber/cross-laminated-timber-clt, https://www.naturallywood.com/engineered-wood-products/cross-laminated-timber-clt/

### ☐ `fact.architecture.future_timber_char_capacity`: unverified

> **Claim:** A wooden member's load-carrying capacity depends on its cross-section, so how much of it chars is the main factor in how long it lasts in a fire; thick timbers keep much of their strength.

- **Concept:** How thick timber survives fire (`concept.architecture.future_timber_char`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L93 “Tall Timber” · `card.architecture.093.c3` (text): Why a thick timber survives a fire / Wood burns, but thick wood burns slowly and predictably. Fire turns its surface to char, and that char insulates the wood inside, slowing the damage. In a standard fire test, wood chars at an average of about 0.6 mm per minute. A timber's strength depends on how much solid wood is left, so a thick one keeps much of its strength while its outside burns away. Here's an analogy: a big log on a campfire, black outside, solid inside.
- **Tested by:**
  - L93 `question.architecture.093.q3`: After 1666, London rebuilt in brick for protection from fire (Level 6). Why can a thick timber column still hold up in a fire? → **Its char insulates the solid wood inside**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The AWC notes that massive wood systems keep significant structural capacity for long periods in fire because they char slowly and predictably. Sources: https://awc.org/resources/introduction-to-cross-laminated-timber/, https://www.westerntimberframe.com/mass-timber-charring-natures-fire-shield/

## Arch (architecture) (Encyclopaedia Britannica)

- **Source:** `source.brit_arch_architecture`
- **URL:** https://www.britannica.com/technology/arch-architecture
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.architecture.arch_centering`: unverified

> **Claim:** While an arch is being built, its voussoirs need support from below, usually temporary wooden centering, until the keystone is set.

- **Concept:** How an arch works (`concept.architecture.stand_arch`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L4 “The Arch” · `card.architecture.004.c1` (text): An arch can't stand up until its very last stone goes in. / Until then, builders prop it up on a temporary wooden frame called centering. Set the top stone, take the frame away, and the whole curve holds itself up. What changed?
  - L4 “The Arch” · `card.architecture.004.c2` (text): Wedges that squeeze together / An arch is built from wedge-shaped blocks called voussoirs, each cut to press firmly against its neighbors. The central one, set last, is the keystone. Weight pressing down forces the wedges together instead of apart, so the whole curve stays in compression. Remember Level 3's problem: stone is weak when stretched. An arch never asks it to stretch.
  - L5 “Domes” · `card.architecture.005.c1` (text): A dome can do something an arch can't: stand while it's half built. / Level 4's arch needed a wooden frame until its keystone went in. A dome can rise ring by ring with no frame at all. The secret is in its circles.
  - L94 “3D-Printed Houses” · `card.architecture.094.c2` (text): No mold needed / Ordinary concrete needs formwork: a temporary structure that holds the wet mix in shape until it hardens. It's the concrete cousin of Level 4's centering, the wooden frame that holds up an arch until the keystone is set. Formwork can take more than half the resources of a concrete structure. A construction printer skips it. Following a digital design, it squeezes concrete through a nozzle and builds the wall layer by layer.
- **Tested by:**
  - L4 `question.architecture.004.q1`: What is the keystone of an arch? → **The central wedge-shaped block, set last**
  - L4 `question.architecture.004.q3`: Compared with Level 3's stone lintel, why can a stone arch span a wider opening? → **Its small blocks are squeezed together, never stretched**
  - L17 `question.architecture.017.q3`: The Colosseum's outer walls are three stories of stone arcades. Which Level 4 idea lets each arch carry its load? → **Its wedge-shaped stones are squeezed together**
  - L18 `question.architecture.018.q3`: The Pont du Gard's arches were built without mortar. What keeps their stones in place? → **Weight squeezing the wedge-shaped stones together**

### ☐ `fact.architecture.arch_thrust`: unverified

> **Claim:** An arch's load produces a diagonal outward force called thrust, which will make the arch collapse unless its supports are massive enough to resist it and carry it into the foundation.

- **Concept:** An arch's thrust (`concept.architecture.stand_arch_thrust`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L4 “The Arch” · `card.architecture.004.c3` (text): The push at the feet / The catch: an arch doesn't only push down. It also pushes outward at its feet, a diagonal force called thrust. Left unchecked, thrust makes the arch collapse, so its supports must be massive enough to resist it and carry it down into the foundation. Here's an analogy: lean two playing cards together on a slippery table. Their bottoms slide apart unless something blocks them.
  - L20 “Checkpoint: Ancient Wonders” · `card.architecture.020.c2` (text): Trabeated and arcuated / A trabeated building is designed with horizontal beams or lintels: Level 3's posts and lintels. An arcuated one has arches: Level 4's wedges. Beams are simple, but stone ones must stay short. Arches of small blocks span much wider openings, but they push outward, so their supports must be massive. The great temples in this chapter each pick a side.
  - L23 “Round Arches and Thick Walls” · `card.architecture.023.c1` (text): Put a stone ceiling on a church, and the walls have to wrestle it. / Romanesque builders roofed their churches with stone vaults. Level 4 already warned what arches do: they push outward. So how do you hold a stone ceiling up without it shoving the walls apart?
  - L23 “Round Arches and Thick Walls” · `card.architecture.023.c2` (text): A tunnel made of arches / Romanesque churches used round arches for windows, doors and arcades, and many roofed the nave with a barrel vault: in effect a continuous row of arches, deep enough to cover a room, like half a tunnel. Every one of those arches pushes out, so a barrel vault must be held in along its entire length by heavy walls with few openings. That's why these churches have massive piers and walls with few windows. Big holes would weaken the very walls doing the holding.
  - L24 “Gothic Cathedrals” · `card.architecture.024.c3` (text): A half arch in the air / Gothic vaults still pushed outward, just as Level 4's thrust says they must, and the supports still had to be massive enough to resist it. The answer was the flying buttress: a half arch that springs from the upper part of the wall and carries the vault's thrust across the aisle to an outer pier. Level 4's massive supports are all still there. They've simply moved outdoors, clear of the wall.
  - L71 “Gaudí” · `card.architecture.071.c3` (text): Columns that lean like trees / Level 4's arches push outward at their feet, a diagonal thrust that massive supports must resist. Gaudí wanted his buildings to stand without buttresses propping them from outside, the way a tree stands. So his piers and columns tilt, leaning along the diagonal thrust they carry. Inside the Sagrada Família they rise like a forest of twisting stone trunks. The lean isn't a wobble. It's the force, made visible.
  - L99 “How to Look at a Building” · `card.architecture.099.c3` (text): Step 2: Find how it stands / Next, ask how it stands. Do thick walls carry the floors, or does a frame? A wall of glass is a giveaway: in a frame building, a skeleton of columns and beams carries the floors, and the outer wall bears only its own weight (Level 8). Spot an arch? Look for the massive supports resisting its outward thrust (Level 4).
- **Tested by:**

  - L23 `question.architecture.023.q3`: Level 4 showed that an arch pushes outward at its feet. Why must a barrel vault have heavy walls along its whole length? → **It is a row of arches, each pushing outward**
  - L24 `question.architecture.024.q3`: Level 4 said an arch's supports must be massive to resist its thrust. Where did Gothic builders put that mass? → **In outer piers linked to the wall by flying buttresses**
  - L43 `question.architecture.043.q3`: Level 4's arch pushes outward at its feet. Where do a yurt's roof poles push outward? → **Where they meet the top of the wall**

### ☐ `fact.architecture.future_buoyancy_displaced`: unverified

> **Claim:** A floating object sinks until the water it displaces weighs as much as it does, and sinks deeper when it is loaded; the upward buoyant force equals the weight of the water displaced.

- **Concept:** Why a concrete house floats (`concept.architecture.future_floating_buoyancy`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L95 “Floating Buildings” · `card.architecture.095.c2` (text): Archimedes moves in / A floating object sinks until the water it pushes aside weighs as much as it does; then the water's upward push holds it up. That's why a lump of clay sinks but the same clay shaped into a boat floats, and why steel ships float too. Shape does the work. So each amphibious house at Maasbommel stands on a large, hollow concrete cube: plenty of room to push water aside.
  - L95 “Floating Buildings” · `card.architecture.095.c4` (fact): Carry in a piano, and the house sits lower. / Level 2's load path ended in the soil. A floating house's path ends in water: the house settles until the water it displaces weighs as much as the house and everything in it. Add a live load, like Level 2's piano, and it sinks a little deeper until the balance returns. Floating homes keep the heavy concrete below and build light on top.
- **Tested by:**
  - L95 `question.architecture.095.q2`: Why can a house on a hollow concrete base float? → **It pushes aside water weighing as much as it does**
  - L95 `question.architecture.095.q3`: Level 2 calls a piano a live load. What happens when one is carried into a floating house? → **The house settles a little lower in the water**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. OpenStax College Physics states Archimedes' principle: the buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced. Sources: https://openstax.org/books/college-physics-2e/pages/11-7-archimedes-principle, https://www.britannica.com/technology/naval-architecture/Weight-and-buoyancy

> **Claim:** Firmness is structural strength, commodity is usefulness to the people who use the building, and delight is beauty.

Miss one and the building fails: a gorgeous house with a leaky roof, or a sturdy box nobody can bear to look at. This chapter is all about the first one.

  - L98 “Design for Everyone” · `card.architecture.098.c4` (fact): Commodity, for everyone. / Level 1's Vitruvius said good building needs commodity: usefulness to the people who use it. ### ☐ `fact.architecture.brick_fired_kiln`: unverified

> **Claim:** Fired brick is burned in a kiln for strength, hardness and heat resistance; at Ur, potters discovered the closed kiln, whose heat could be controlled.

- **Concept:** Mud brick and fired brick (`concept.architecture.stand_brick`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L6 “Stone, Brick and Wood” · `card.architecture.006.c2` (comparison): Three old materials, three trade-offs: Stone (Great strength when squeezed; Weak when stretched, so lintels stay short; Resists fire) vs Brick (Sun-dried mud brick: at least 6,000 years old; Fired in a kiln: strong and hard; Made small enough for one person to handle) vs Wood (Strong for its weight; Easy to cut and shape; Burns)
  - L6 “Stone, Brick and Wood” · `card.architecture.006.c4` (fact): Baking a brick changes it. / The first bricks were mud, shaped and dried in the sun. Fire them in a kiln and they gain strength, hardness and resistance to heat. At Ur, in Mesopotamia, potters discovered the closed kiln, in which the heat could be controlled. And ancient brickmakers kept each brick small enough for one person to handle easily: small, easy-to-carry blocks, just what Level 4's arches need.
  - L12 “Ziggurats” · `card.architecture.012.c3` (text): A raincoat with vents / Every ziggurat had a core of mud brick and a skin of baked brick. At Ur, the core took several million sun-dried bricks. The facing bricks were mortared with bitumen, a natural tar, to make a waterproof surface: Level 6's kiln-fired brick, hard and strong, doing the weather work. The skin was also pierced by weeper holes that let water evaporate from the core. A raincoat, with vents.
- **Tested by:**
  - L6 `question.architecture.006.q1`: What turns a mud brick into a fired brick? → **Burning it in a kiln**
  - L44 `question.architecture.044.q3`: Level 6's bricks were fired in a kiln. Why does unfired adobe have to be kept dry? → **It never permanently hardens, and grows weaker the wetter it gets**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Fired bricks, baked in kilns, are more durable than sun-dried bricks; kiln-fired brick appears in Mesopotamia. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brick
- **Weak evidence:** one-page, weak-pages (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.architecture.beam_bending`: unverified

> **Claim:** When a beam bends under a load, its top is squeezed in compression and its bottom is stretched in tension.

- **Concept:** Why beams bend, and why stone beams stay short (`concept.architecture.stand_beam_bending`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L3 “Posts and Beams” · `card.architecture.003.c3` (text): The beam's problem: it bends / Load a beam and it sags a little. Its top is squeezed in compression while its underside is stretched in tension: Level 2's two forces, in one piece. Stone and brick are brittle and weak in tension, so a long stone beam is in trouble along its underside. That's why stone and brick can only make short lintels. / Try it: bend a ruler. The top face squeezes and the bottom face stretches.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: How Buildings Stand” · `card.architecture.010.c4` (comparison): How Buildings Stand: three ways to carry weight: Posts and beams (Posts are squeezed; the beam is stretched underneath (Level 3); So stone lintels stay short) vs Arches and domes (Wedges squeezed together (Level 4); They push outward; a dome's lower rings stretch (Level 5)) vs Frames (A skeleton carries the floors; walls hold only themselves (Level 8); Steel takes the stretch, in frames and in concrete (Levels 7 and 8))
  - L13 “The Pyramids of Giza” · `card.architecture.013.c4` (fact): The top compartment has a pointed roof. / The highest of the five compartments has a gabled roof: huge limestone blocks set in leaning pairs, like the two sides of a house roof, helping to bear the weight above. Remember Level 3: a flat stone beam is stretched along its underside. Leaning blocks press against each other instead, a bit like Level 4's arch wedges. A flat ceiling, a stack of slabs, and a point on top.
  - L72 “Frank Lloyd Wright” · `card.architecture.072.c3` (text): The cantilever: a beam held at one end / A cantilever is a beam supported at only one end, with the other end free. (A diving board is one.) It bends the opposite way from Level 3's lintel. A lintel is stretched along its underside; a loaded cantilever is stretched along its upper half and squeezed along its lower half. Concrete handles stretching badly, so Fallingwater's concrete terraces carry steel reinforcing rods inside.
- **Tested by:**
  - L3 `question.architecture.003.q2`: Why can brick and stone make only short lintels? → **A loaded beam's underside is stretched, and stone is weak in tension**
  - L4 `question.architecture.004.q3`: Compared with Level 3's stone lintel, why can a stone arch span a wider opening? → **Its small blocks are squeezed together, never stretched**
  - L6 `question.architecture.006.q3`: Level 3's stone lintels had to stay short. What did the Greeks gain by using wooden beams instead? → **Fewer supports and more open space inside**
  - L7 `question.architecture.007.q3`: Like Level 3's lintel, a concrete beam over a doorway is stretched along its underside. What is the usual fix? → **Cast steel bars inside to take the tension**
  - L8 `question.architecture.008.q3`: Level 3 showed that a loaded beam is stretched along its underside. Why does that make steel a good beam material? → **It has high tensile strength**
  - L13 `question.architecture.013.q3`: Level 3 showed that a loaded stone beam is stretched along its underside. Why is that a worry in the King's Chamber? → **Its flat stone ceiling is a lintel under a mountain**
  - L14 `question.architecture.014.q3`: Using Level 3's lintels, why does Karnak's Great Hypostyle Hall need so many columns? → **Stone roof beams must stay short, so posts crowd in**
  - L100 `question.architecture.100.q2`: A long stone lintel over a wide gap cracks along its underside. Why there? → **The underside is stretched, and stone is weak in tension**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. In a simply supported beam under load, the top fibers are in compression and the bottom fibers in tension. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bending

### ☐ `fact.architecture.hanging_vs_supporting`: unverified

> **Claim:** A cable holding up a hanging load is in tension, while a post or tower carrying weight down to the ground is in compression.

- **Concept:** Tension and compression (`concept.architecture.stand_tension_compression`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L2 “Why Buildings Stand Up” · `card.architecture.002.c4` (fact): Every piece of that path is being squeezed or stretched. / Engineers name two basic forces. Compression pushes and squeezes; tension pulls and stretches. A post carrying weight down to the ground is squeezed. A cable holding up a hanging load is stretched. Keep both words handy: the rest of this chapter is about which parts get squeezed, which get stretched, and which materials can take it.
  - L45 “Houses on Stilts” · `card.architecture.045.c3` (text): Standing on legs / Stilts are Level 2's load path made visible. The whole house, and everyone in it, pushes down through the posts into the ground, so every stilt is in compression, like any post carrying weight. The Alpine builders planted theirs firmly: they burned each pile's end to a point, drove it deep into the mud, packed heavy stones around it and laid a platform of tree trunks and branches on top.
  - L51 “Bridges” · `card.architecture.051.c3` (text): Two ways to hang a road / For longer spans, engineers hang the road. In a suspension bridge the deck hangs from curved cables in tension, which carry the load to towers and to anchorages at each end. Remember Level 10's hanging chain? That's the cable. A cable-stayed bridge skips the big curve: nearly straight diagonal cables run from the deck directly to the towers. France's Millau Viaduct, opened in 2004, is one, strung across the whole Tarn valley by architect Norman Foster and engineer Michel Virlogeux.
- **Tested by:**
  - L2 `question.architecture.002.q3`: In a stack of books on a table, the bottom book carries all the others. Which force is it under? → **Compression, because it is squeezed**
  - L10 `question.architecture.010.q3`: How Buildings Stand recap: a hanging chain is in tension. Which force runs along the arch you get by flipping its shape? → **Compression, running along the curve**
  - L45 `question.architecture.045.q3`: Level 2 named two basic forces. Which one is a stilt holding up a house under? → **Compression, like any post carrying weight**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Suspension-bridge cables carry the deck in tension while towers carry it to the ground in compression; a hanging chain is in tension. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/technology/suspension-bridge, https://plus.maths.org/content/matjhs-minute-catenary

## Building construction (Encyclopaedia Britannica)

- **Source:** `source.brit_building_construction`
- **URL:** https://www.britannica.com/technology/building-construction
- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.architecture.tension_compression_defined`: unverified

> **Claim:** Compression is a pushing, squeezing force and tension a pulling, stretching one; structures must resist both.

- **Concept:** Tension and compression (`concept.architecture.stand_tension_compression`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L2 “Why Buildings Stand Up” · `card.architecture.002.c4` (fact): Every piece of that path is being squeezed or stretched. / Engineers name two basic forces. Compression pushes and squeezes; tension pulls and stretches. A post carrying weight down to the ground is squeezed. A cable holding up a hanging load is stretched. Keep both words handy: the rest of this chapter is about which parts get squeezed, which get stretched, and which materials can take it.
  - L3 “Posts and Beams” · `card.architecture.003.c3` (text): The beam's problem: it bends / Load a beam and it sags a little. Its top is squeezed in compression while its underside is stretched in tension: Level 2's two forces, in one piece. Stone and brick are brittle and weak in tension, so a long stone beam is in trouble along its underside. That's why stone and brick can only make short lintels. / Try it: bend a ruler. The top face squeezes and the bottom face stretches.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: How Buildings Stand” · `card.architecture.010.c2` (text): As hangs the chain / Unscrambled, Hooke's anagram said: "As hangs the flexible line, so but inverted will stand the rigid arch." A hanging chain is in tension, with every force running along its curve. Flip the shape and those forces become compression, still running along the curve, so the arch doesn't bend or buckle. Level 2's two forces turn out to be mirror images.
  - L96 “Building on the Moon” · `card.architecture.096.c3` (text): The inside-out building / On Earth, gravity squeezes buildings: Level 2's compression. A pressurized Moon habitat is mainly in tension instead, its walls pushed outward and stretched by the air inside. Here's an analogy: a balloon's skin, pulled tight by the air it holds. To protect it, engineers suggest a thick outer layer of regolith, the Moon's loose, broken soil and rock, to dampen temperature swings and shield against radiation.
- **Tested by:**
  - L2 `question.architecture.002.q3`: In a stack of books on a table, the bottom book carries all the others. Which force is it under? → **Compression, because it is squeezed**
  - L10 `question.architecture.010.q3`: How Buildings Stand recap: a hanging chain is in tension. Which force runs along the arch you get by flipping its shape? → **Compression, running along the curve**
  - L45 `question.architecture.045.q3`: Level 2 named two basic forces. Which one is a stilt holding up a house under? → **Compression, like any post carrying weight**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Engineering references define tension as a stretching force and compression as a squeezing force. Sources: https://plus.maths.org/content/matjhs-minute-catenary, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compression_(physics)

### ☐ `fact.architecture.marvel_cable_stayed_defined`: unverified

> **Claim:** In a cable-stayed bridge, nearly straight diagonal cables in tension carry the deck's weight directly to one or more towers.

- **Concept:** Cable-stayed bridges (`concept.architecture.marvel_cable_stayed`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L51 “Bridges” · `card.architecture.051.c3` (text): Two ways to hang a road / For longer spans, engineers hang the road. In a suspension bridge the deck hangs from curved cables in tension, which carry the load to towers and to anchorages at each end. Remember Level 10's hanging chain? That's the cable. A cable-stayed bridge skips the big curve: nearly straight diagonal cables run from the deck directly to the towers. France's Millau Viaduct, opened in 2004, is one, strung across the whole Tarn valley by architect Norman Foster and engineer Michel Virlogeux.
- **Tested by:**
  - L51 `question.architecture.051.q2`: How does a cable-stayed bridge differ from a suspension bridge? → **Straight cables run from the deck to the towers**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Cable-stayed bridges connect the deck directly to towers by cables; unlike suspension bridges they need no main cable between anchorages. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cable-stayed_bridge

In reinforced concrete, steel bars take the tension and the concrete takes the compression.

  - L59 `question.architecture.059.q3`: Unreinforced brick has little or no steel inside. From Level 7, what job does steel do inside reinforced concrete? → **It takes the tension, the stretching**
  - L72 `question.architecture.072.q3`: Fallingwater's concrete terraces sagged for decades. Why did the 2001-2002 repair use tightened steel cables? → **Steel takes tension, which concrete resists poorly**
  - L94 `question.architecture.094.q3`: Level 7's concrete beams hide steel bars to take the tension. Why is that harder in a 3D-printed wall? → **Layer-by-layer printing makes steel hard to add**

That's awkward when vault ribs cross a rectangular bay, because the short sides, long sides and diagonals all want different heights. A pointed arch escapes the trap. ### ☐ `fact.architecture.fallingwater_post_tension`: unverified

> **Claim:** In 2001-2002, engineers anchored high-strength steel cables beneath Fallingwater and tightened them along its beams, stopping the sag.

- **Concept:** Fallingwater's sagging cantilevers and their repair (`concept.architecture.masters_wright_fallingwater_sag`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L72 “Frank Lloyd Wright” · `card.architecture.072.c4` (fact): Fallingwater's terraces sagged. / By 1955 the Kaufmanns had measured them tilting down about four inches. Decades later, in 2001 and 2002, engineers anchored bundles of high-strength steel cable into the concrete below the house, ran them along the big beams under the living room and tightened them. The sagging stopped. Level 7's lesson, applied late: when concrete is stretched, steel has to take the tension.
- **Tested by:**
  - L72 `question.architecture.072.q3`: Fallingwater's concrete terraces sagged for decades. Why did the 2001-2002 repair use tightened steel cables? → **Steel takes tension, which concrete resists poorly**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Britannica and engineering press describe the 2002 post-tensioning with steel cables that halted the deflection. Sources: https://www.britannica.com/topic/Fallingwater, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallingwater

### ☐ `fact.architecture.gothic_flying_buttress_defined`: unverified

> **Claim:** A flying buttress is a half arch that carries the thrust of a roof or vault from the upper part of a wall across an aisle to an outer pier.

- **Appears in:**
  - L24 “Gothic Cathedrals” · `card.architecture.024.c3` (text): A half arch in the air / Gothic vaults still pushed outward, just as Level 4's thrust says they must, and the supports still had to be massive enough to resist it. The answer was the flying buttress: a half arch that springs from the upper part of the wall and carries the vault's thrust across the aisle to an outer pier. Level 4's massive supports are all still there. They've simply moved outdoors, clear of the wall.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Temples and Churches” · `card.architecture.030.c3` (comparison): Temples and Churches: three ways to raise a holy roof: Domes (Hagia Sophia: pendentives turn a square into a circle (Level 21); St. Peter's: checked with a hanging chain, bound in iron (Level 29)) vs Stone skeletons (Pointed arches and ribs carry the vault (Level 24); Flying buttresses take the thrust outside (Level 24)) vs Sacred mountains (Angkor Wat's towers are Meru's peaks (Level 26); Kandariya Mahadeva's towers refer to Meru too (Level 28))
- **Tested by:**
  - L24 `question.architecture.024.q1`: What does a Gothic flying buttress carry from the upper wall across the aisle to an outer pier? → **The outward thrust of the vault**
  - L24 `question.architecture.024.q3`: Level 4 said an arch's supports must be massive to resist its thrust. Where did Gothic builders put that mass? → **In outer piers linked to the wall by flying buttresses**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. A flying buttress transmits the thrust of a vault or roof from the upper wall to an outer support across an intervening space. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_buttress

### ☐ `fact.architecture.gothic_pinnacle_weight`: unverified

> **Claim:** A pinnacle often tops the pier of a flying buttress, adding weight and stability; the flying buttress evolved from simpler hidden supports and made high-ceilinged Gothic churches possible.

- **Concept:** The flying buttress (`concept.architecture.gothic_flying_buttress`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L24 “Gothic Cathedrals” · `card.architecture.024.c4` (fact): The little spires on top are there for their weight. / A pier holding a flying buttress is often crowned with a pinnacle. It adds weight, and weight makes the pier more stable against the push arriving from the vault. The flying buttress itself evolved from simpler supports hidden from view, and its extra supporting power is what made the high ceilings of Gothic churches possible. Decoration, yes, but decoration with a job.

### ☐ `fact.architecture.hindu_garbhagriha_defined`: unverified

> **Claim:** The garbhagriha, often translated "womb house", is the innermost and most sacred sanctuary of a Hindu temple, housing the main image or emblem of its deity.

  - L28 “Hindu Temples” · `card.architecture.028.c1` (text): A Hindu temple's tallest tower stands over its smallest room. / From outside you see a soaring tower, sometimes a whole range of them. Underneath the highest peak is a small chamber for the deity. The tower and the room are one idea, told in stone.
  - L28 “Hindu Temples” · `card.architecture.028.c2` (text): The womb house / The heart of a Hindu temple is the garbhagriha, often translated "womb house". It's the innermost and most sacred sanctuary, housing the main image or emblem of the temple's deity, and it's small. ### ☐ `fact.architecture.timeline_home_insurance`: unverified

> **Claim:** Chicago's Home Insurance Building (1884-85) is generally considered the first tall building held up by an iron and steel skeleton frame.

- **Concept:** How building changed: a timeline (`concept.architecture.stand_building_timeline`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L1 “Architecture in One Level” · `card.architecture.001.c4` (timeline): How building changed, in six steps: At least 6,000 years ago: Sun-dried mud brick, one of the first building materials; Prehistory to Rome: Posts and beams: stone laid across uprights; 118–128 CE: Rome's Pantheon rises under a great concrete dome; 1420–1436: Brunelleschi builds Florence Cathedral's dome; 1851: London's Crystal Palace: prefabricated iron and glass; 1884–85: Chicago's Home Insurance Building: an iron and steel skeleton
  - L8 “Steel and Glass” · `card.architecture.008.c4` (text): Why steel suits the frame / Stone and cast iron share a weakness: both are weak when stretched. Steel isn't. It has high tensile strength, which suits Level 3's beams, stretched along their undersides. In 1884–85, Chicago's Home Insurance Building rose on an iron and steel skeleton; it's generally considered the first tall building held up that way. Later chapters take that skeleton all the way to the sky.

### ☐ `fact.architecture.arch_compression`: unverified

> **Claim:** Weight pressing down on an arch forces its voussoirs together instead of apart, keeping the masonry in compression.

- **Concept:** How an arch works (`concept.architecture.stand_arch`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L4 “The Arch” · `card.architecture.004.c2` (text): Wedges that squeeze together / An arch is built from wedge-shaped blocks called voussoirs, each cut to press firmly against its neighbors. The central one, set last, is the keystone. Weight pressing down forces the wedges together instead of apart, so the whole curve stays in compression. Remember Level 3's problem: stone is weak when stretched. An arch never asks it to stretch.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: How Buildings Stand” · `card.architecture.010.c4` (comparison): How Buildings Stand: three ways to carry weight: Posts and beams (Posts are squeezed; the beam is stretched underneath (Level 3); So stone lintels stay short) vs Arches and domes (Wedges squeezed together (Level 4); They push outward; a dome's lower rings stretch (Level 5)) vs Frames (A skeleton carries the floors; walls hold only themselves (Level 8); Steel takes the stretch, in frames and in concrete (Levels 7 and 8))
  - L18 “Aqueducts” · `card.architecture.018.c4` (fact): The Pont du Gard stands without mortar. / Where the Nîmes aqueduct crossed the Gard River, the Romans built the Pont du Gard: three tiers of arches, with the water channel along the top. It was built without mortar. Level 4 explains how that works: weight presses each arch's wedge-shaped stones together, keeping the whole curve in compression.
  - L54 “Tunnels” · `card.architecture.054.c4` (text): An arch that goes all the way round / Once it's open, a tunnel has one job: not getting crushed. The ground presses on it from every side, not just from above. So a tunnel's basic shape is a continuous arch: the curve of Level 4, carried all the way round. Just as an arch's wedges squeeze together under weight, a tunnel's ring is pressed together by the ground around it.
- **Tested by:**
  - L4 `question.architecture.004.q1`: What is the keystone of an arch? → **The central wedge-shaped block, set last**
  - L4 `question.architecture.004.q3`: Compared with Level 3's stone lintel, why can a stone arch span a wider opening? → **Its small blocks are squeezed together, never stretched**
  - L17 `question.architecture.017.q3`: The Colosseum's outer walls are three stories of stone arcades. Which Level 4 idea lets each arch carry its load? → **Its wedge-shaped stones are squeezed together**
  - L18 `question.architecture.018.q3`: The Pont du Gard's arches were built without mortar. What keeps their stones in place? → **Weight squeezing the wedge-shaped stones together**
  - L54 `question.architecture.054.q3`: A tunnel is basically a continuous arch. As with Level 4's arch, what does the surrounding pressure do to its ring? → **Squeezes it together, in compression**
  - L60 `question.architecture.060.q3`: Engineering Marvels recap: which Chapter 1 shape do both a tunnel's lining and an arch dam borrow? → **The arch**
  - L86 `question.architecture.086.q3`: Some Metropolitan Railway trenches were roofed with a brick arch. As Level 4 explained, how does an arch carry the street above? → **Weight squeezes its wedge-shaped blocks together**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. An arch carries loads primarily in compression. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arch

  - L51 “Bridges” · `card.architecture.051.c3` (text): Two ways to hang a road / For longer spans, engineers hang the road. In a suspension bridge the deck hangs from curved cables in tension, which carry the load to towers and to anchorages at each end. Remember Level 10's hanging chain? That's the cable. A cable-stayed bridge skips the big curve: nearly straight diagonal cables run from the deck directly to the towers. > **Claim:** In a mosque, the mihrab, a niche for the imam who leads the prayer, points to the qibla, the direction of Mecca that Muslims face in prayer.

- **Appears in:**
  - L22 “Great Mosques” · `card.architecture.022.c1` (text): A mosque is designed around a direction. / Before anyone chooses columns or domes, a mosque has to know one thing: which way Mecca lies. Everything else can change, and at Córdoba and Istanbul, it did.

Mosques follow a different rule: the mihrab faces Mecca, whatever direction that is (Level 22). And while the other temples around it face east, Angkor Wat faces west. A holy building has a front door, but it also has a direction.

> **Claim:** In a mosque, the mihrab, a niche for the imam who leads the prayer, points to the qibla, the direction of Mecca that Muslims face in prayer.

- **Appears in:**
  - L22 “Great Mosques” · `card.architecture.022.c1` (text): A mosque is designed around a direction. / Before anyone chooses columns or domes, a mosque has to know one thing: which way Mecca lies. Everything else can change, and at Córdoba and Istanbul, it did.
  - L22 “Great Mosques” · `card.architecture.022.c2` (text): The wall that points to Mecca / Muslims face Mecca to pray, and a mosque is built to match. That direction is the qibla, and the wall facing it holds the mihrab, a niche for the imam who leads the prayer. Beside it stands the minbar, a pulpit of steps for the preacher. Outside rises the minaret, the tower from which the muezzin gives the call to prayer five times each day. Think of a mosque as a building with a compass built in.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Temples and Churches” · `card.architecture.030.c2` (text): Which way to face / Orientation, from Latin oriens, "the rising sun", is a building's position on the east-west axis. Mosques follow a different rule: the mihrab faces Mecca, whatever direction that is (Level 22). And while the other temples around it face east, Angkor Wat faces west. A holy building has a front door, but it also has a direction.

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The mihrab is a niche in the mosque wall indicating the qibla, the direction of the Kaaba in Mecca that Muslims face when praying. ### ☐ `fact.architecture.concrete_weak_tension`: unverified

> **Claim:** Plain concrete resists compression well but not tension; in reinforced concrete, steel bars take the tension and the concrete takes the compression.

- **Concept:** Modern and reinforced concrete (`concept.architecture.stand_reinforced_concrete`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L7 “Concrete” · `card.architecture.007.c4` (text): Modern concrete, and a gardener's tubs / Modern concrete is bound with portland cement, which Joseph Aspdin made in 1824 by burning and grinding limestone and clay. But concrete shares Level 3's stone problem: strong when squeezed, weak when stretched. The fix is usually credited to Joseph Monier, a Paris gardener who reinforced his concrete tubs with iron mesh and patented the idea in 1867. In reinforced concrete, steel bars take the tension and the concrete takes the compression.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: How Buildings Stand” · `card.architecture.010.c4` (comparison): How Buildings Stand: three ways to carry weight: Posts and beams (Posts are squeezed; the beam is stretched underneath (Level 3); So stone lintels stay short) vs Arches and domes (Wedges squeezed together (Level 4); They push outward; a dome's lower rings stretch (Level 5)) vs Frames (A skeleton carries the floors; walls hold only themselves (Level 8); Steel takes the stretch, in frames and in concrete (Levels 7 and 8))
  - L12 “Ziggurats” · `card.architecture.012.c4` (fact): Some ziggurats were reinforced with reeds. / At Aqar Quf in Iraq, after every eight or nine courses of bricks, the builders laid a layer of reed matting bedded in sand and gravel. Plaited reed ropes run right through the tower from side to side as reinforcement, and the matting kept the structure from slumping sideways when it got wet. Here's an analogy: Level 7's steel bars do a similar job inside concrete today.
  - L72 “Frank Lloyd Wright” · `card.architecture.072.c4` (fact): Fallingwater's terraces sagged. / By 1955 the Kaufmanns had measured them tilting down about four inches. Decades later, in 2001 and 2002, engineers anchored bundles of high-strength steel cable into the concrete below the house, ran them along the big beams under the living room and tightened them. The sagging stopped. Level 7's lesson, applied late: when concrete is stretched, steel has to take the tension.
  - L94 “3D-Printed Houses” · `card.architecture.094.c4` (fact): Printing still has Level 7's problem. / Concrete is weak when stretched, so builders usually cast steel bars inside to take the tension. In a printed wall that's hard: building layer by layer makes conventional steel reinforcement difficult to add, and the joints between layers are weaker than solid cast concrete. The Eindhoven house was printed as 24 separate elements in a factory, then trucked to the site and set on a foundation.
- **Tested by:**
  - L7 `question.architecture.007.q3`: Like Level 3's lintel, a concrete beam over a doorway is stretched along its underside. What is the usual fix? → **Cast steel bars inside to take the tension**
  - L12 `question.architecture.012.q3`: The plaited reed ropes inside the Aqar Quf ziggurat act as reinforcement. What does that job in Level 7's modern concrete? → **Steel bars**
  - L59 `question.architecture.059.q3`: Unreinforced brick has little or no steel inside. From Level 7, what job does steel do inside reinforced concrete? → **It takes the tension, the stretching**
  - L72 `question.architecture.072.q3`: Fallingwater's concrete terraces sagged for decades. Why did the 2001-2002 repair use tightened steel cables? → **Steel takes tension, which concrete resists poorly**
  - L94 `question.architecture.094.q3`: Level 7's concrete beams hide steel bars to take the tension. Why is that harder in a 3D-printed wall? → **Layer-by-layer printing makes steel hard to add**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Concrete is strong in compression and weak in tension; embedded steel rebar carries the tensile stresses. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforced_concrete

### ☐ `fact.architecture.frame_skeleton`: unverified

> **Claim:** In a frame building, a skeleton of columns and beams carries the floors, and the outer wall bears only its own weight and hangs on the frame.

- **Concept:** Load-bearing walls versus a frame (`concept.architecture.stand_frame_structure`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L8 “Steel and Glass” · `card.architecture.008.c2` (text): Walls that carry, or a frame that carries / Until now in this chapter, walls and posts did the carrying: each wall held up the floors above it, on Level 2's load path. A frame building splits the jobs. A skeleton of columns and beams carries the floors, and the outer wall only has to hold up itself. Here's an analogy: your bones hold you up, and your skin just wraps you. Once a wall carries nothing but itself, it can be thin, even glass.
  - L10 “Checkpoint: How Buildings Stand” · `card.architecture.010.c4` (comparison): How Buildings Stand: three ways to carry weight: Posts and beams (Posts are squeezed; the beam is stretched underneath (Level 3); So stone lintels stay short) vs Arches and domes (Wedges squeezed together (Level 4); They push outward; a dome's lower rings stretch (Level 5)) vs Frames (A skeleton carries the floors; walls hold only themselves (Level 8); Steel takes the stretch, in frames and in concrete (Levels 7 and 8))
  - L25 “Walls of Light” · `card.architecture.025.c2` (text): A skeleton with windows / Level 8's frame building splits the jobs: a skeleton carries the floors, and the outer wall only holds itself. A Gothic cathedral works the same way in stone. Ribs, piers and flying buttresses do the carrying, so the wall between them can open into larger windows. At Chartres, mainly built after 1194, the architect dropped the gallery level and used specially designed flying buttresses to enlarge the clerestory, the windowed wall rising above the aisle roofs. After Chartres, great churches were meant to be dominated by glass set high up.
  - L47 “Timber Frames” · `card.architecture.047.c3` (text): Or build a skeleton / Timber-framed houses do the opposite. In a medieval timber-framed building, the frame of timbers is the load-bearing structure, and the spaces between the timbers only need filling to keep the weather out. A common filling was wattle and daub: small timbers woven into a lattice, then daubed with mud, dung, water and straw. Sound familiar? It's Level 8's frame building, where the skeleton carries the floors and the walls hold only themselves.
  - L49 “The Modern House” · `card.architecture.049.c4` (fact): A steel frame frees the walls. / Remember Level 8: once a skeleton of columns and beams carries the floors, the outer wall bears only its own weight and hangs on the frame. The Eames House's steel frame was up within 16 hours, so its walls never had to carry the floors: the frame did. And Level 8 showed where that leads: a wall that carries only itself can be thin, even glass.
  - L61 “The First Skyscrapers” · `card.architecture.061.c3` (text): The Chicago school / Those ideas came from a group of architects and engineers now called the Chicago school: William Le Baron Jenney, Daniel Burnham, John Root, Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan. Together they developed the skyscraper. Jenney designed the Home Insurance Building (1884–85), generally considered the first tall building held up by an iron and steel skeleton: Level 8's frame, taken up high. Chicago has been called the birthplace of modern architecture.
  - L66 “Glass Towers” · `card.architecture.066.c2` (text): A wall that hangs / Level 8 split the jobs: the frame carries the floors, and the outer wall holds up only itself, hanging on the frame. That outer skin is called a curtain wall: a nonbearing wall of glass, metal or masonry attached to the building's structural frame. The name fits. Like a curtain, it hangs from something else and holds nothing up.
  - L70 “Checkpoint: Skyscrapers” · `card.architecture.070.c4` (comparison): Skyscrapers: what it takes to stand, rise and stay put: Stand (A steel frame carries the floors (Level 61); The glass or stone skin just hangs on it (Level 66)) vs Rise (Otis's brake made elevators safe (Level 62); After 1857, more than five stories became practical) vs Stay put (Shape changes confuse the wind (Levels 64-65); Dampers like Taipei 101's steel ball steady the sway)
  - L73 “Le Corbusier” · `card.architecture.073.c2` (text): Dom-ino: a house as a kit / In 1914 he drew the Dom-ino system: three concrete floor slabs, six posts and a staircase. That's the whole thing. As in Level 8's frame, the skeleton carries the floors, so no wall has to hold anything up. Walls can go anywhere, windows can run the full length of the front, and the module can be repeated again and again. The rest of his career grew out of this kit.
  - L99 “How to Look at a Building” · `card.architecture.099.c3` (text): Step 2: Find how it stands / Next, ask how it stands. Do thick walls carry the floors, or does a frame? A wall of glass is a giveaway: in a frame building, a skeleton of columns and beams carries the floors, and the outer wall bears only its own weight (Level 8). Spot an arch? Look for the massive supports resisting its outward thrust (Level 4).
- **Tested by:**
  - L8 `question.architecture.008.q2`: In a frame building, why can the outer wall be thin, or even glass? → **The skeleton carries the floors; the wall holds only itself**
  - L15 `question.architecture.015.q3`: The Colossus of Rhodes was bronze plates fastened to an iron framework. Which Level 8 idea does that echo? → **An inner skeleton carries the load; the skin wraps it**
  - L25 `question.architecture.025.q3`: In Level 8's frame building, a skeleton carries the floors. What plays the skeleton's part in a Gothic cathedral? → **Ribs, piers and flying buttresses**
  - L47 `question.architecture.047.q3`: Level 8 compared load-bearing walls with frames. Which is a medieval timber-framed house? → **A frame: timbers carry the load, the filling just fills**
  - L50 `question.architecture.050.q7`: How Homes Are Built milestone: which Chapter 1 idea lets a timber house get away with walls of mud and straw? → **A frame carries the load, so infill holds only itself**
  - L73 `question.architecture.073.q3`: Level 8 split the jobs of wall and frame. In Le Corbusier's Dom-ino system, what carries the floors? → **Six posts, with three concrete slabs and a staircase**
  - L74 `question.architecture.074.q3`: The Bauhaus workshop wing in Dessau is wrapped in glass. According to Level 8, what makes a glass outer wall possible? → **A frame carries the floors, so the wall holds only itself**
  - L99 `question.architecture.099.q3`: Reading a building: its outer walls are all glass. Using Level 8, what is most likely carrying its floors? → **A skeleton frame of columns and beams**

### ☐ `fact.architecture.gothic_pointed_arch_spans`: unverified

> **Claim:** Pointed arches escape the rigid geometry of semicircular arches, whose height is set by their width: arches of different spans can rise to the same height.

- **Concept:** Why Gothic builders used the pointed arch (`concept.architecture.gothic_pointed_arch`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L24 “Gothic Cathedrals” · `card.architecture.024.c2` (text): The adjustable arch / A round arch is stuck with rigid geometry: its height is set by its width. That's awkward when vault ribs cross a rectangular bay, because the short sides, long sides and diagonals all want different heights. A pointed arch escapes the trap. Sharpen or relax the point, and arches of different spans rise to the same height, meeting neatly at the top. With pointed arches and rib vaults like Durham's, Gothic builders could cover far more complicated plans. Think of it as an arch that comes in adjustable sizes.
  - L30 “Checkpoint: Temples and Churches” · `card.architecture.030.c3` (comparison): Temples and Churches: three ways to raise a holy roof: Domes (Hagia Sophia: pendentives turn a square into a circle (Level 21); St. Peter's: checked with a hanging chain, bound in iron (Level 29)) vs Stone skeletons (Pointed arches and ribs carry the vault (Level 24); Flying buttresses take the thrust outside (Level 24)) vs Sacred mountains (Angkor Wat's towers are Meru's peaks (Level 26); Kandariya Mahadeva's towers refer to Meru too (Level 28))
- **Tested by:**
  - L24 `question.architecture.024.q2`: Why did Gothic builders prefer pointed arches for vaulting rectangular bays? → **Arches of different spans can rise to the same height**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Pointed arches can be raised as high over a short span as over a long one, unlike round arches, so ribs of rectangular bays meet at one height. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointed_arch, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rib_vault
- **Weak evidence:** weak-pages (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.architecture.romanesque_barrel_vault_defined`: unverified

> **Claim:** A barrel vault is in effect a continuous series of arches; it thrusts like an arch and must be buttressed along its entire length by heavy walls with limited openings.

- **Concept:** The Romanesque barrel vault and thick walls (`concept.architecture.romanesque_barrel_vault`)

Every one of those arches pushes out, so a barrel vault must be held in along its entire length by heavy walls with few openings. That's why these churches have massive piers and walls with few windows. Big holes would weaken the very walls doing the holding.
- **Tested by:**

### ☐ `fact.architecture.romanesque_groin_vault_defined`: unverified

> **Claim:** Two barrel vaults crossing at right angles form a groin vault; in a row, groin vaults can cover long rectangular spaces, and their thrust gathers at the four corners, so only those points need buttressing.

- **Concept:** The groin vault (`concept.architecture.romanesque_groin_vault`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L23 “Round Arches and Thick Walls” · `card.architecture.023.c3` (text): Cross two tunnels / Cross two barrel vaults at right angles and you get a groin vault. Repeated in a row, groin vaults can cover a long rectangular space. The trick is where the push goes: it gathers at the four corners, so only those points need buttressing, and the wall between them no longer has to be massive. Here's an analogy: a table carries its top on four legs, not on solid sides.
- **Tested by:**

Level 6 said wood is strong for its weight; tall timber puts that strength to work, and plans for the fire.

  - L51 “Bridges” · `card.architecture.051.c3` (text): Two ways to hang a road / For longer spans, engineers hang the road. In a suspension bridge the deck hangs from curved cables in tension, which carry the load to towers and to anchorages at each end. Remember Level 10's hanging chain? That's the cable. A cable-stayed bridge skips the big curve: nearly straight diagonal cables run from the deck directly to the towers. France's Millau Viaduct, opened in 2004, is one, strung across the whole Tarn valley by architect Norman Foster and engineer Michel Virlogeux.

## Architectural Importance (Durham Cathedral) (Durham World Heritage Site (Durham University))

- **Source:** `source.durham_whs_architecture`

### ☐ `fact.architecture.durham_rib_vault`: unverified

> **Claim:** Durham Cathedral is the earliest known example of stone ribs forming pointed arches to support a vault; the ribs let the filling be thinner and lighter, and the vault has stood for 900 years.

- **Concept:** Durham Cathedral's rib vaults (`concept.architecture.romanesque_durham_ribs`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L23 “Round Arches and Thick Walls” · `card.architecture.023.c4` (fact): Durham Cathedral's ceiling hides a stone skeleton. / Durham Cathedral in England, begun in 1093, is an outstanding Romanesque church. Its builders set stone ribs, forming pointed arches, to support the vault: the earliest known example. The ribs carry the vault at critical points, so the stone filling between them could be thinner and lighter. The vault has stood for 900 years. Next level, Gothic builders take that skeleton and run.
  - L24 “Gothic Cathedrals” · `card.architecture.024.c2` (text): The adjustable arch / A round arch is stuck with rigid geometry: its height is set by its width. That's awkward when vault ribs cross a rectangular bay, because the short sides, long sides and diagonals all want different heights. A pointed arch escapes the trap. Sharpen or relax the point, and arches of different spans rise to the same height, meeting neatly at the top. With pointed arches and rib vaults like Durham's, Gothic builders could cover far more complicated plans. Think of it as an arch that comes in adjustable sizes.
- **Tested by:**
  - L23 `question.architecture.023.q1`: What did Durham Cathedral's builders set under its vault, the earliest known example of the idea? → **Stone ribs forming pointed arches**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Durham's nave has the earliest surviving pointed rib vault, an experimental model for later Gothic building. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_Cathedral, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rib_vault
- **Weak evidence:** weak-pages (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.architecture.future_esa_catenary_cells`: unverified

> **Claim:** The ESA study's shell was a weight-bearing catenary dome with hollow, closed-cell walls like bird bones, and the team printed a 1.5-tonne building block as a demonstration.

- **Concept:** ESA's printed lunar base study (`concept.architecture.future_lunar_printed_base`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L96 “Building on the Moon” · `card.architecture.096.c4` (fact): In 2013, ESA tested printing a Moon base from Moon soil. / ESA and partners including the architects Foster + Partners studied whether a 3D printer could build a lunar base from regolith. The design: an inflatable, pressurized dome to shelter astronauts, covered by a robot-printed regolith shell. The shell was a weight-bearing catenary dome with hollow, closed cells like bird bones. A catenary is a hanging chain's curve: flip it and you get Level 10's arch. The team printed a 1.5-tonne demonstration block. It was a study, not a base.
- **Tested by:**

  - L72 “Frank Lloyd Wright” · `card.architecture.072.c3` (text): The cantilever: a beam held at one end / A cantilever is a beam supported at only one end, with the other end free. (A diving board is one.) It bends the opposite way from Level 3's lintel. A lintel is stretched along its underside; a loaded cantilever is stretched along its upper half and squeezed along its lower half. Concrete handles stretching badly, so Fallingwater's concrete terraces carry steel reinforcing rods inside.

### ☐ `fact.architecture.marvel_tacoma_lessons`: unverified

> **Claim:** The collapse spurred research into how wind acts on bridges; the replacement, opened in 1950, used a web truss, and later suspension bridges were designed with its lessons.

  - L60 “Checkpoint: Engineering Marvels” · `card.architecture.060.c2` (text): The force nobody gave a path / Its deck was narrow, just two lanes, and stiffened by solid plate girders instead of open trusses. Those girders didn't absorb the wind's gusts, and the deck began to twist, each swing larger than the last. The replacement, opened in 1950, used a web truss, and the collapse spurred research into how wind acts on bridges. Later suspension bridges were designed with its lessons.
- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The 1950 replacement used open stiffening trusses; the failure made aerodynamics central to long-span bridge design. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacoma_Narrows_Bridge, https://www.asce.org/about-civil-engineering/history-and-heritage/historic-landmarks/tacoma-narrows-bridges

### ☐ `fact.architecture.marvel_tunnel_continuous_arch`: unverified

> **Claim:** A tunnel's basic shape is a continuous arch: because it must withstand pressure from all sides, the arch goes all the way around.

- **Concept:** A tunnel as an arch all the way round (`concept.architecture.marvel_tunnel_ring_arch`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L54 “Tunnels” · `card.architecture.054.c4` (text): An arch that goes all the way round / Once it's open, a tunnel has one job: not getting crushed. The ground presses on it from every side, not just from above. So a tunnel's basic shape is a continuous arch: the curve of Level 4, carried all the way round. Just as an arch's wedges squeeze together under weight, a tunnel's ring is pressed together by the ground around it.
  - L60 “Checkpoint: Engineering Marvels” · `card.architecture.060.c3` (comparison): Engineering Marvels: every force needs a path: Across a gap (Beams bend, arches push, cables hang (Level 51); Arch dams push the water into the valley sides (Level 55)) vs Rock and water (A tunnel is an arch that goes all the way round (Level 54); Water pushes hardest at depth, so dams thicken at the base (Level 55)) vs The ground itself (Piles carry loads down to firm ground (Level 58); Base isolators let the ground move beneath (Level 59))
- **Tested by:**
  - L54 `question.architecture.054.q3`: A tunnel is basically a continuous arch. As with Level 4's arch, what does the surrounding pressure do to its ring? → **Squeezes it together, in compression**
  - L60 `question.architecture.060.q3`: Engineering Marvels recap: which Chapter 1 shape do both a tunnel's lining and an arch dam borrow? → **The arch**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Tunnel linings are designed as arches or rings so ground pressure is carried mainly in compression around the section. Sources: https://www.pcepurnia.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/TUNNELS-TYPESANDIMPORTANCE.pdf

Its 1999 charter says you can spot it by a way of building shared across a community, a local character that answers the environment, and know-how passed on informally, from builder to builder. So who designed all these homes? / Igloos, gers, adobe pueblos, stilt houses: most of this chapter's homes are what ICOMOS calls vernacular building, "the traditional and natural way by which communities house themselves." The interiors of Egyptian temples were lined with columns covered by stone lintels. And Level 3 showed why stone lintels stay short: stone is weak when stretched. Short beams mean crowded posts.   - L14 “Egyptian Temples” · `card.architecture.014.c3` (text): A tall aisle with windows / The columns aren't all alike. ## Riddle solved: Why was Roman concrete so durable? (MIT News)

- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-24 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.architecture.lime_clasts_healing`: unverified

> **Claim:** In the study, water reaching a clast through a crack dissolved calcium that refilled the crack as calcium carbonate; hot-mixed test samples sealed their cracks within two weeks.

- **Concept:** Self-healing Roman concrete (2023 findings) (`concept.architecture.stand_lime_clasts`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L7 “Concrete” · `card.architecture.007.c3` (fact): Roman concrete may patch its own cracks. / That's the finding of a 2023 MIT-led study of concrete from the Roman site of Privernum. Its little white lumps, called lime clasts, were long blamed on sloppy mixing. The study says they formed when builders mixed in hot quicklime. When a crack reaches a clast and water gets in, dissolved calcium refills the crack as calcium carbonate. Test samples made this way sealed their cracks within two weeks. These are one study's findings, not a verdict on every Roman building.
- **Tested by:**

- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. The paper reports crack-healing by calcium carbonate recrystallization; cracked hot-mixed samples healed within two weeks while controls did not. Sources: https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.add1602

### ☐ `fact.architecture.dome_hoop_forces`: unverified

> **Claim:** Besides forces running down its curve, a dome carries hoop forces in horizontal rings; they let a dome be built ring by ring without centering, which an arch cannot do.

- **Concept:** A dome's hoop forces (`concept.architecture.stand_dome_hoops`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L5 “Domes” · `card.architecture.005.c1` (text): A dome can do something an arch can't: stand while it's half built. / Level 4's arch needed a wooden frame until its keystone went in. A dome can rise ring by ring with no frame at all. The secret is in its circles.
  - L5 “Domes” · `card.architecture.005.c3` (text): Rings that squeeze, rings that stretch / A dome has a trick an arch lacks. Besides the forces running down its curve, it carries hoop forces around it, in horizontal rings. Near the top the rings squeeze, so each finished ring holds itself in place. Lower down, the rings are stretched instead, and masonry hates stretching. So masonry domes tend to crack along lines running from top to rim, splitting into slices (think orange segments) whose bases lean outward.
- **Tested by:**
  - L5 `question.architecture.005.q2`: Why can a dome rise ring by ring without a wooden frame? → **Each finished ring is squeezed tight and holds itself**
  - L10 `question.architecture.010.q5`: How Buildings Stand recap: where in a masonry dome do the hoop forces turn into stretching? → **In the lower part, toward the rim**
  - L19 `question.architecture.019.q3`: Level 5 said a masonry dome's hoop forces stretch toward its base. Where did the Pantheon's dome crack? → **Top to rim, in the lower half**
  - L42 `question.architecture.042.q3`: Like Level 5's domes, an igloo rises without a wooden frame. How do its blocks manage it? → **They climb a spiral, leaning inward until they close into a dome**
  - L100 `question.architecture.100.q4`: Why did Brunelleschi bind Florence's dome with tie rings? → **To hold in the lower part, where hoops stretch**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Masonry dome analyses describe meridional and hoop (latitudinal ring) forces; hoop compression near the crown stabilizes each course. Sources: https://www.academia.edu/3278819/Tension_Ring_in_Masonry_Domes
- **Weak evidence:** one-page (revisit first)

### ☐ `fact.architecture.live_loads`: unverified

> **Claim:** Live loads are transient and can change: people, sofas, pianos, books and cars, plus loads from the weather; wind counts as a sideways (lateral) live load.

- **Concept:** Dead loads and live loads (`concept.architecture.stand_loads`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L2 “Why Buildings Stand Up” · `card.architecture.002.c2` (text): Dead loads and live loads / Engineers sort weight into two kinds. Dead loads are permanent: the structure's own weight plus its roofing, flooring, pipes and inside walls. Live loads come and go: people, sofas, pianos, books, cars. Weather counts as a live load too, and wind pushes sideways rather than down. A floor has to be ready for both, including the day your friend moves in with a piano.
  - L64 “Wind and Tall Buildings” · `card.architecture.064.c2` (text): Pushed across the wind / Level 2 called wind a sideways live load. Here's the sneaky part. As wind flows past a tall building, swirls of air called vortices form and break away, first from one side, then the other. Each one tugs the building. So it gets pushed and pulled across the wind's direction, not just along it.
  - L92 “Living Walls” · `card.architecture.092.c4` (fact): Milan's trees wear seatbelts. / Level 2 said wind is a live load that pushes sideways, and a tree on a balcony catches plenty of it. The engineers at Arup ran two wind tunnel test campaigns. Medium and large trees are tied on with safety cables in case a trunk breaks, and the biggest trees in the windiest spots sit in steel cages that hold their root-balls down.
  - L95 “Floating Buildings” · `card.architecture.095.c4` (fact): Carry in a piano, and the house sits lower. / Level 2's load path ended in the soil. A floating house's path ends in water: the house settles until the water it displaces weighs as much as the house and everything in it. Add a live load, like Level 2's piano, and it sinks a little deeper until the balance returns. Floating homes keep the heavy concrete below and build light on top.

## Neuschwanstein Castle: an example of Historicism (Bayerische Schlösserverwaltung)

### ☐ `fact.architecture.neuschwanstein_copies_nothing`: unverified

> **Claim:** Neuschwanstein copies no existing building: it is an example of historicism, combining motifs from the Wartburg with castles from medieval book illustrations.

- **Concept:** Neuschwanstein: a knight's castle from a stage set (`concept.architecture.neuschwanstein_historicism`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L39 “Fairy-Tale Castles” · `card.architecture.039.c2` (text): A castle from a stage set / Ludwig wrote to Richard Wagner, whom he greatly admired, that he would build 'in the authentic style of the old German knights' castles'. The designs came from stage sets by the Munich scene painter Christian Jank, turned into plans by the architect Eduard Riedel. Neuschwanstein copies no real building. It mixes motifs from the Wartburg castle with castles from medieval book illustrations, a style called historicism.
- **Tested by:**
  - L39 `question.architecture.039.q2`: Why is Neuschwanstein called historicism rather than a real medieval castle? → **It copies no real castle, mixing old motifs anew**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. Wikipedia says the inspiration came partly from Ludwig's 1867 visit to the reconstructed Wartburg and describes the castle as a work of historicism. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neuschwanstein_Castle

- **License:** reference_only · **Accessed:** 2026-09-25 · **Source record checked (URL/licence):** no

### ☐ `fact.architecture.chain_tension_arch_compression`: unverified

> **Claim:** A hanging chain is in tension along its curve; turned upside down, those forces become compression along the arch, so it does not bend or buckle.

- **Concept:** Hooke's hanging chain (`concept.architecture.stand_hanging_chain`)
- **Appears in:**
  - L10 “Checkpoint: How Buildings Stand” · `card.architecture.010.c2` (text): As hangs the chain / Unscrambled, Hooke's anagram said: "As hangs the flexible line, so but inverted will stand the rigid arch." A hanging chain is in tension, with every force running along its curve. Flip the shape and those forces become compression, still running along the curve, so the arch doesn't bend or buckle. Level 2's two forces turn out to be mirror images.
  - L71 “Gaudí” · `card.architecture.071.c2` (text): Design it upside down / Remember Level 10's hanging chain? Gaudí turned it into a design tool. He hung networks of cords and loaded them with small bags of weight, standing in for the stone each arch would carry. A hanging cord is in pure tension. Turn its shape upside down and the forces become compression, running along the curve. He worked the method out for a church at the Colònia Güell, near Barcelona, then carried it into the Sagrada Família.
  - L96 “Building on the Moon” · `card.architecture.096.c4` (fact): In 2013, ESA tested printing a Moon base from Moon soil. / ESA and partners including the architects Foster + Partners studied whether a 3D printer could build a lunar base from regolith. The design: an inflatable, pressurized dome to shelter astronauts, covered by a robot-printed regolith shell. The shell was a weight-bearing catenary dome with hollow, closed cells like bird bones. A catenary is a hanging chain's curve: flip it and you get Level 10's arch. The team printed a 1.5-tonne demonstration block. It was a study, not a base.
- **Tested by:**
  - L10 `question.architecture.010.q1`: In Hooke's 1675 anagram, what does a hanging chain's shape become when turned upside down? → **A rigid arch that stands**
  - L10 `question.architecture.010.q3`: How Buildings Stand recap: a hanging chain is in tension. Which force runs along the arch you get by flipping its shape? → **Compression, running along the curve**
  - L71 `question.architecture.071.q3`: Gaudí's weighted-cord models put Level 10's hanging-chain idea to work. What is that idea? → **A hanging shape in tension, flipped, stands as an arch in compression**
  - L96 `question.architecture.096.q3`: Foster + Partners shaped ESA's printed lunar shell as a catenary dome. Which Level 10 idea does that shape use? → **A hanging chain, flipped, stands as an arch**
  - L100 `question.architecture.100.q5`: ESA's 2013 Moon base study used a catenary dome. In Hooke's terms from Level 10, what is a catenary arch? → **A hanging chain's curve, turned upside down**
- **Fact-check (2026-09-25):** corroborated. An inverted catenary arch carries its own weight in pure compression, mirroring the hanging chain in tension. Sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catenary
- **Weak evidence:** one-page, weak-pages (revisit first)
